blocks.text: …your garage is sitting on top of a twelve-inch high-pressure gas main. It has to come down."
Dave's mouth opened and closed. "My uncle approved the permit," he finally said.
"Yes, sir," the inspector said. "That's the other reason we're here."

It turned out Dave's garage had always been close to the easement. The original builder had kept it just inside the legal line. But when Dave poured a new concrete pad to "square off" his yard and move the fence, his crew also extended the garage foundation four inches to make room for a workshop. His uncle at the county had signed off on the permit without sending anyone to inspect it.
Building over a gas easement isn't a paperwork issue. If the main ever needed emergency repair, crews would have to dig straight through his garage floor.

And the heavy concrete pad was sitting directly on top of a pipe that carried gas to half the neighborhood. The utility company had flagged it when I sent them my survey, the photo of the iron pin, and a copy of the permit.

Dave was ordered to remove the extension, and the new pad above the main, at his own expense, under the supervision of the gas company. He also had to tear out the fence on my side of the line. My attorney sent him the 1984 survey and a polite letter. The fence came down within a week.
His uncle was suspended from the county permit office while the state reviewed every permit he'd signed in the last five years. Three other properties had been approved the same way.
I had an arborist check them, and Dave paid that bill too.

It's been quiet on our street since then. Dave mostly keeps to himself. Last month, though, he knocked on my door, holding a cutting from his rose garden in a pot. "The pin was under it," he said. "Figured it's technically yours." I planted it by the oaks. It's doing fine.
